title: Vasseur responds to gossip about his future
excerpt:
Any Ferrari Formula 1 Team Principal is always in the spotlight, and in the case of Fred Vasseur the gossip ramped up over the Baku weekend in the wake of former Red Bull chief Christian Horner’s suggestion that he would welcome a role with the Maranello-based team.

Not surprisingly, that fuelled speculation that Vasseur is under pressure, and that Horner was a possible candidate to replace him.

Just before the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia weekend kicked off, Ferrari moved to dampen the speculation with a media call, where it was made clear that Vasseur had the full support of the team – and, most importantly, both its Chairman John Elkann and Chief Executive Officer Benedetto Vigna.

Then on Thursday in Sepang, Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton both backed their boss, with the former calling the chat about Vasseur “not nice” and “disrespectful”.

On Friday, Vasseur appeared in the press conference alongside Alpine's Flavio Briatore and Williams' James Vowles, with the Frenchman asked why it was felt the Ferrari media call had been necessary.

“You have to ask your colleagues,” said the Frenchman. “When you see the noise and all the rumours in the press all the week, I think as a team we need to work in serenity. And it was absolutely not the case.

“And I think the statement, it was mandatory to do something, or it could have been the same this weekend. But honestly, the big issue that we have today is to put stability, put serenity into the team, the focus that we need to have – and not to have this kind of question all day.”

While Hamilton backed Vasseur on Thursday, calling him a “fantastic leader”, he also indicated the Ferrari structure could be improved, noting that “there are changes that I would make, but I'm not going to talk about what those are.”

When reminded of Hamilton’s comments and asked if he felt changes were also required below him, Vasseur made it clear that any team has to evolve, referencing a previous answer from Briatore about bolstering Alpine’s technical leadership.

“First of all, the structure of the team, I think as Flavio said before, in the individual recruitment, at least, it's a [never-ending] story,” he insisted. “I think that you have to improve. I think it's the DNA of what we are doing to not take a success as a final situation, but to try to improve in the good and the bad moments.

“And honestly, the dynamic that we have, we have recruited a lot, as have the other teams.

“On the comment of Lewis, I think it would be a mistake to finger point someone or something or whatever. In the good moment, we are winning as a team, in the bad moment, we are suffering as a team, and I don't want to speak about single individual or whatever.

“We had a good beginning of the season. But for sure, it's not enough. We want to get more, we want to win more, we want to win the championship. But at the end of the day, we had a positive start, we are struggling the last couple of races, but we are hoping to come back with development.”

Pressed further on whether organisational changes were needed he said: “Honestly, the relationship that I have with my bosses, Benedetto and John, is a very good one. We are in daily contact, and I can't complain at all about the organisation.

“But for sure, you always want to get more. You always want to do more. You always want to recruit more. But I think it's true for me, and it's true for everybody on the grid that you always want to do more because of the DNA of what we are doing. But honestly, it has nothing to do with the organisation.”

Asked about the intense focus that’s always applied to a Ferrari boss, Vasseur stressed that he knew that would come with the territory.

BARRETTO: Why Ferrari have moved to shield Vasseur

“When you take the role, you know the positive and the negative side of the job,” he said. “I was expecting something like this. What is sometimes a bit unfair, and when you put someone under the bus, I'm there also to defend my team, my guys. As I said before, when we are winning, we are winning as a team.

“But when we are struggling, I'm there to defend them, to all of them. And I think it's the right attitude from everybody, from them to defend the Team Principal, from me to defend them when we are struggling.

“Now honestly, I knew that what I will get [with this job], I'm not surprised at all. But sometimes the attacks are a bit personal – and this is not good.”

title: Who has the edge in Sepang after a too-close-to-call Friday?
excerpt:
Formula 1's return to Sepang for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia got off to a competitive start, with the top four teams within four tenths of a second of each other in second practice. But who is showing signs of emerging as the one to beat as degradation dominated the radio and post-session chatter?

Let's cut to the chase. Who are the favourites?

I'm not trying to dodge the question, honest – but it's really too close to call according to our data.

title: What the teams said – Friday in Malaysia
excerpt:
The drivers and teams report back on all the action from Friday practice for the 2026 Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia at the Sepang International Circuit.

Oct 02, 2026 12:04pm UTC

Red Bull

Max Verstappen topped the opening session for Red Bull by a comfortable margin, and with Isack Hadjar in P3, the car looked strong out of the box. There were some question marks about overheating, but the same could be said for most of the field. In the second session, Hadjar impressed again with p2, while Verstappen was fourth, but crucially was the only driver not to run the soft tyre, thus setting his lap time on the mediums.

The bad news for Hadjar is it has been confirmed he will take a five-place grid drop for Sunday’s race for fitting a new ICE.

Max Verstappen - FP1: 1:37.520, P1; FP2: 1:37.785, P4

“I think we had a pretty decent start today. We began well; the track was quite tricky as it was very hot with a lot of degradation, so there are a few things, particularly with the tyres, that we will need to analyse tonight. It was warmer in FP2 and a different programme that we were running, so it is quite difficult to compare the progress between the two sessions. There are still a few things we need to understand better ahead of tomorrow, but we have had two positive sessions, which is good.”

Isack Hadjar - FP1: 1:38.303, P3; FP2: 1:37.627, P2

“A very good start to the weekend in terms of competitiveness. The track is very challenging and the conditions are tough, so I feel there's still a lot of lap time to find. I'm not completely happy with the balance of the car yet, but I'm super happy with our overall competitiveness. Tomorrow, I think Qualifying is going to be very short and sharp, with only a few laps available on the tyres, but I'm looking forward to it. I think we have a good car this weekend and that we can fight at the front.”

Pierre Wache, Technical Director

“It’s been a challenging day here at Sepang, but also a very interesting one. It has been quite demanding for the drivers and the car because of the heat, but I think we have made a good start to the weekend.

"The track surface was extremely dusty, and the grip evolved a lot throughout the day, but we made a good start in the opening session, evaluating the package we brought to Baku and focusing on different types of corners, particularly in the low speed. Overall, it seems to be working better than what we brought last weekend.

"In the second session, we had expected rain but, when that didn’t appear, we prioritised the long run on the Medium tyre, as gaining data on tyre behaviour and degradation will be the most important thing for the rest of the weekend. In the end, that meant we ran out of time for Max to run the Soft, but Isack had the opportunity, and that was valuable. Isack had a few issues in the session with balance, but we will do our best to iron those out overnight. After that, in terms of relative performance, it is very difficult to judge, but so far, we are happy with where we are.”

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Max Verstappen of the Netherlands driving the (3) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Sona Maleterova/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Isack Hadjar of France driving the (6) Oracle Red Bull Racing RB22 Red Bull Ford Powertrains on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Ferrari

It was a steady start for Ferrari, who had both cars in the top six in the opening session. Roll on the second session, and Charles Leclerc wound up on top of the timing sheets with an impressive flying lap on the softs. Lewis Hamilton could not quite match his team mate and wound up fifth, three tenths back as the field started to close up. Hamilton did find himself in hot water for blocking Gabriel Bortoleto at one point, the stewards opting to give him a warning for that moment.

Charles Leclerc - FP1: 1:38.367, P4; FP2: 1:37.528, P1

"We had a good day and learned a lot about this track, but there’s still plenty of work ahead of us until Sunday. Our performance was good, however, we mustn’t underestimate our competitors as I think they have more to show tomorrow. The field is tight, the track was quite dirty and slippery today, and I expect to see quite a significant evolution between today and qualifying. Degradation is going to be the main talking point of the weekend. Even a small difference in how you take some of the corners can make a huge difference in terms of degradation, so it should make for an interesting race."

Lewis Hamilton - FP1: 1:38.590, P6; FP2: 1:37.833, P5

"It was a challenging day overall, with very little grip available on track. Finding the right balance wasn’t easy but that appeared to be a common theme across the field. Throughout the sessions we explored a couple of different set up directions, and now the focus is on understanding the data and identifying the right compromise. We don’t seem too far off the pace but we know there’s still work to do to put the car in a better place for tomorrow."

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Charles Leclerc of Monaco driving the (16) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Lewis Hamilton of Great Britain driving the (44) Scuderia Ferrari SF-26 kicks up dust on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Mercedes

George Russell started his weekend in Malaysia well, looking strong in the opening session. He finished second behind Verstappen, but while his one-lap pace was quick, Russell was concerned about tyre wear in his Mercedes. As for Kimi Antonelli, he was a little bit off the pace as his weekend began in slightly more circumspect fashion. Both made a mistake through the final corner on their one flying lap on the softs in FP2, and thus did not set fully representative lap times. But if they can nail that tricky final corner, they look right in the mix here.

Kimi Antonelli - FP1: 1:38.580, P5; FP2: 1:38.060, P8

"We have had a decent first day on track here in Malaysia. The PETRONAS Sepang International Circuit is incredible to drive! It is fast and flowing so it’s super cool. We were able to complete lots of running across both sessions and worked through a full programme too. We gathered plenty of data, both useful for understanding the new update we’ve brought here and for helping us make improvements over the rest of the weekend here in Malaysia.

"We’ve still got a lot of work to do though. The Red Bulls look the fastest on both the single lap and the long run, with McLaren and Ferrari also competitive on higher fuel in particular. The track was quite low grip today and it is likely that it will improve into Saturday and Sunday. We will work hard tonight to find improvements overnight and do our best come qualifying tomorrow afternoon."

George Russell - FP1: 1:37.903, P2; FP2: 1:38.020, P7

"It was a really cool experience to get out on track for the first time here at the PETRONAS Sepang International Circuit. I’ve never driven here before and it’s great to do so given how iconic this place is. The support we’ve had here as a team is also amazing so thanks for all the fans for coming out today and over the weekend.

"With these warm conditions, combined with the aggressive tarmac and the characteristics of the circuit, the tyre degradation throughout practice was high. That was as we expected coming into the weekend but with the amount of overheating on the tyres, it slightly neutralises the performance of any extra downforce we’ve added with our update. The cars are operating in quite a different window to what we usually do, and I don’t think we quite got ours into the place that we needed today. We will look to get on top of that overnight and hopefully, if we do so, we can be in the fight at the front for the rest of the weekend."

Andrew Shovlin, Trackside Engineering Director

"We were running the latest update package on both cars today but rather than seeing the step in lap time that we had hoped for, we have been chasing a tricky balance and a fair amount of tyre overheating. We had a few test items on the cars in FP1 that might have clouded the situation but for FP2, we had both cars in a representative configuration, and it looked like we were still trailing, especially to the Red Bull.

"We've got some good ideas for setup changes to investigate during the overnight simulator work and will continue to analyse today's data to understand why we seem to lack a bit of a pace. we're optimistic that with such a new package, these analyses will bear some fruit. The headline times are not especially representative, and we should be able to make some relatively easy progress on the single lap pace. Our concern is more the long run where we seemed unusually offset on pace and that is going to be the more challenging problem to solve."

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: George Russell of Great Britain driving the (63) Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team W17 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Peter Bonnington, Race Engineer of Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team and Andrea Kimi Antonelli of Italy and Mercedes AMG Petronas F1 Team talk in the garage during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

McLaren

McLaren did not look to be chasing outright pace in FP1, instead using the session to test out different rear wing configurations on each car. Whatever they discovered, their drivers were evenly matched with just 0.017s between them. They did run a more conventional programme in FP2, with Lando Norris impressing on his flying lap to grab third, just over a tenth off the pace. Oscar Piastri was a few places further back, but it certainly looks like McLaren have the speed to compete for pole tomorrow, especially if they can dial in their set-up that tiny bit more.

Lando Norris - FP1: 1:39.293, P12; FP2: 1:37.665, P3

"An interesting first day here at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia. Nice to get our first laps in around this circuit, it's a fun track and an interesting challenge in terms of layout and track surface. We're struggling more than we'd like to, but we made some progress going into FP2. We've still got quite a bit more to solve if we want to be competitive, but we'll look at the data this evening and see what we can do going into FP3 and Qualifying tomorrow."

Oscar Piastri - FP1: 1:39.276, P11; FP2: 1:37.899, P6

“That’s Friday at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia done. It was a reasonable day for us. From FP1 into FP2, we made a solid amount of progress, which meant we finished the day well. Our Quali sims and longer runs felt pretty good. But we still have a lot to find overnight and a lot more to understand about racing here. The true long-run performance across the grid, including for us, is still a bit of an unknown for everyone, but it feels like we could be in the mix.

“The circuit is a cool one to drive, but we’re finding the grip and high tyre degradation are really challenging. We need to understand both better overnight to put us in a better position ahead of Qualifying. Our goal is to build on today’s positive momentum and extract as much performance as possible to ensure we’re competitive.”

Randy Singh, Senior Director, Racing

“We found the track conditions quite surprising today. It was a lot rougher and had more grip than our initial forecasts suggested. This presented a challenge in FP1, where we struggled to get the car into an optimal window. However, the team did a fantastic job, both here at the circuit and back at the factory, to analyse the data and dial the car in much better for the second session. We felt far more comfortable in FP2 and made a solid step forward.

“Tyre degradation was the main talking point, and it was consistently high all day, which will definitely be a major factor in the race. The hot, abrasive surface is really tough on the tyres. From a strategy perspective, the high degradation naturally pushes things towards a two-stop, as the numbers make a three-stop very difficult without other factors like a Safety Car. We still have plenty of work ahead of us to fine-tune everything for Qualifying, but we are focused on exploiting the full potential of our package.”

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Lando Norris of Great Britain driving the (1) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Rudy Carezzevoli/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Oscar Piastri of Australia driving the (81) McLaren MCL40 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Alpine

Pierre Gasly was quick from the off, topping the midfield with a very strong lap on the soft tyre at a track he has raced at before – unlike his Racing Bulls rivals. As for the Frenchman's Alpine team mate Franco Colapinto, he was down the order but is set for grid penalties here. The first is five-places for causing that collision in Baku, and the other is 10-places after it was confirmed he has taken another ICE.

Gasly finished in the top 10 again in the second session, so it looks like an entertaining fight between the Frenchman and Liam Lawson awaits tomorrow.

Pierre Gasly - FP1: 1:38.715, P7; FP2: 1:38.588, P10

“It's good to be back in Malaysia and it always brings nice memories back for me having made my debut at this track in 2017. Nine years later, we are back, and it is safe to say not much has changed with the track still enjoyable to drive and the conditions still very hot and very humid, which brings its challenges inside the car. I would say it's been a decent Friday for us where we are in the mix inside the top ten on the timesheets. The track was generally low grip, as expected, and it's clear that it's going to be tough on the tyres. Our car is in a good place, and we just built things up throughout the day, trying different ideas on both high and low fuel, as normal for a Friday with a few tweaks and improvements to make. We're well prepared and we're looking forward to taking on the rest of the weekend.”

Franco Colapinto - FP1: 1:40.531, P19; FP2: 1:43.391, P22

“We had a specific plan for the day on my side of the garage, and executed it well, with our focus firmly on high fuel running and optimising race pace. With the grid penalties from Baku, and also changing some power unit components here, we know that we'll have to pass cars and try to make our way through the field on Sunday. So, it makes a lot of sense to get in the best possible shape for the race, as we know that even if we were to make it to Q3, we will be towards the back anyway. We tried a lot of things and different set-ups and the pace looked relatively competitive and comparable to others. It was nice coming to a new track also, which is a lot of fun to drive, even on high fuel. It will be a challenge for everyone with tyre degradation, with the heat and roughness of the asphalt. It's easy to overheat the tyres which should make the race interesting with possible different strategy options. This may also help given we'll be starting lower down the field, so an added variable could be beneficial.”

Steve Nielsen, Managing Director

“Firstly, it's been a great job by a number of people to have this event prepared and ready. Personally, alongside many in the sport, I thoroughly enjoy being in Malaysia and racing at this amazing track. We ran very different programmes with both drivers today and, in the end, we are satisfied with the work we have been able to complete. Franco ran high fuel in both sessions with an eye on preparing for Sunday's race. He has taken new power unit components for this race which brings a 10-place grid penalty and adds to the 5-place penalty he received for last weekend's incident. We knew at some point we would have to take a penalty for power unit components, like some of our rivals, and we felt this track might be optimal for overtaking and allows more of an opportunity for Franco to work his way through the field, like we saw him do in Monza on his way to the points. He has done a good job today to collect data on high fuel and to help understand the tyres, which is important for Sunday. Pierre was on a more conventional Friday Practice programme and he's been, in general, happy with his day and how the car felt. The grip is particularly low here, the asphalt is also quite harsh, so it gives everyone an extra element to consider, not to mention the weather as we all keep an eye on the sky for potential rain at any given moment, such is the nature of racing in Sepang at this time of year.”

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Pierre Gasly of France driving the (10) Alpine F1 A526 Mercedes on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Sona Maleterova/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Franco Colapinto of Argentina and Alpine F1 prepares to drive during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Racing Bulls

Arvid Lindblad is set for a back of the grid start this weekend after taking on a raft of new power unit components, so he ran two sets of softs in FP1 with his programme set to look a little different to usual. Liam Lawson went for the more common medium – soft programme, and both were quick, finishing in the top 10. The Kiwi racer was in the top 10 again in FP2, while Lindblad fell back slightly but had an entertaining fight with Bortoleto, those two having a little race to see how easy overtaking is here.

Arvid Lindblad - FP1: 1:39.197, P9; FP2: 1:38.678, P11

"We’ve had a good couple of practice sessions today. This track is quite different to the others we’ve been to recently, although funnily enough, it’s actually quite similar to Bahrain. Looking ahead to tomorrow, the pressure is off a little bit, which means I can go out there and have a bit of fun. So far, I’m really enjoying this track because there are plenty of opportunities around here, and the rain can be very unpredictable. Tyre degradation will also be a big talking point, so we’ll see what happens as there’s likely to be a mixture of strategies as all the teams continue to collect data.”

Liam Lawson - FP1: 1:39.106, P8; FP2: 1:38.496, P9

"It's been a fairly positive day here at the Bahrain GP. The track is fun to drive but very hard on tyres, particularly given the fact it hasn't been resurfaced in a few years. It's also extremely hot here in Malaysia, which is physically tough. However, our training and preparation should put us in a strong position ahead of Qualifying tomorrow, where tyre management will be key."

Alan Permane, Team Principal

"First of all, it’s good to be back in Malaysia, Kuala Lumpur is a great city and the circuit will produce an exciting weekend, I’m sure. It’s been a positive day for us today, we’re happy with the performance of both cars and feel we made a step up in between the sessions. The track is a lot smoother than we anticipated, so we made some set-up changes ahead of FP2 to make the most of those conditions. Arvid’s engine change was something we knew we would need to do in the next few races, and we felt this was the most strategic place to do it. With the tyre deg being quite high, there's certainly some overtaking possibilities to be had, so we feel like we've made the right decision. It will certainly be a challenge for him to fight his way through the pack and into the points from the back, but it’s not impossible.”

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Arvid Lindblad of Great Britain driving the (41) Visa Cash App Racing Bulls VCARB 03 RB Ford leads Gabriel Bortoleto of Brazil driving the (5) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Michael Potts/LAT Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Liam Lawson of New Zealand driving the (30) Visa Cash App Racing Bulls VCARB 03 RB Ford on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Mark Sutton - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Audi

Both Audi drivers had moments in FP1, straddling the kerbs and getting it all a bit wrong. But as the grip improved, they were able to extract lap time and Nico Hulkenberg even finished the session in the top 10. The German fell back slightly in FP2, while Gabriel Bortoleto had a couple more moments. First much to his frustration, the Brazilian had to abort a flying run after coming up behind Hamilton who was on the racing line. Then he got on the kerbs after trying a move on Lindblad, before following his rival through a number of corners as he eventually lined up an overtake through Turn 3.

But Bortoleto stopped out on track late on with an apparent gearbox issue, not the ideal way for his Friday to end.

Nico Hulkenberg - FP1: 1:39.211, P10; FP2: 1:39.109, P13

"Coming back to Sepang after so many years meant there was plenty to learn again, and the heat definitely added another challenge. We worked through the programme and gathered a lot of information, but there are still a few areas we need to understand a bit better. We'll go through everything overnight and see where we can find a bit more grip and balance."

Gabriel Bortoleto - FP1: 1:39.548, P13; FP2: 1:39.051, P12

“It was an interesting day, and thankfully the issue we had at the end of FP2 didn’t cost us time. We had a few items to test going from FP1 to FP2, and, overall, we can be quite satisfied with our work. There are still some areas where we can improve, so we’ll work through the data tonight and try to make a few steps forward for tomorrow. But overall, it was a good day and a positive start to the weekend.”

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Gabriel Bortoleto of Brazil driving the (5) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Clive Mason/Getty Images)

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Nico Hulkenberg of Germany driving the (27) Audi F1 Team R26 on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Sona Maleterova/Getty Images)

Haas

Esteban Ocon pipped his team mate in the opening session but had one hairy moment fighting with Sainz towards the end of the session. The Frenchman attempted to overtake, but ran wide over the kerbs as he got on the dusty part of the track, just managing to avoid the grass. He was again the quicker of the two Haas drivers in FP2, seemingly having the edge on Ollie Bearman here. But Haas need to find a few tenths if they want to battle towards the front of the midfield.

Esteban Ocon – FP1: 1:40.158, P15; FP2: 1:39.361, P14

“It was a positive day. First of all, it’s an amazing track to drive again. I remembered it back then as awesome, but driving it again is pure joy every lap. I had fun today, it’s been positive, and we improved the car from FP1 to FP2. Although we still have work to do tonight, we look healthy on the car-side, and it’s performing as it should, so it’s been positive and we need to keep going like that.”

Oliver Bearman - FP1: 1:40.311, P16; FP2: 1:39.706, P16

“It’s been a tough day for us, to be honest. We looked a bit less competitive than what we were probably expecting on low-fuel. On high-fuel, it looks a bit better, but in general, it’s been a tough day for us. On my side, I’ve been learning the track as well and I feel like I’ve made progress, but in FP2, I felt a bit of a lack in confidence, which adds up to a lot of lap time around here. I’m confident we can do a better job tomorrow.”

Ayao Komatsu, Team Principal

“It was a bit of a tricky Friday. On Esteban’s side of the garage it was pretty clean, he did a good job. Of course, we’ve got things to improve but it was a clean pair of sessions. The same cannot be said on Ollie’s side of the garage, where I think we’ve still got this issue with parts, where putting a certain part or a different part doesn’t necessarily behave exactly the same. We had very different feedback across the garage in FP1, and Ollie was much happier in FP1 compared to FP2, and that wasn’t down to track conditions. We really have to dive into this one – we have some ideas, but tonight we need to solve it, because we could then get to the limit of this package and fight in Q2. If we don’t do that, we’ll be out in Q1, so it’s critical that we find out what’s going on with Ollie’s car.”

KUALA LUMPUR, MALAYSIA - OCTOBER 02: Esteban Ocon of France driving the (31) Haas F1 VF-26 Ferrari on track during practice ahead of the F1 Grand Prix of Bahrain in Malaysia at Sepang Circuit on October 02, 2026 in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia. (Photo by Bryn Lennon - Formula 1/Formula 1 via Getty Images)

Aston Martin

title: FIA removes serious point of jeopardy overnight at Sepang
excerpt:
The FIA has moved the pit-entry bollard at the Sepang International Circuit ahead of FP3 for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia after drivers raised concerns about the procedure during Friday's running.

The bollard had initially been positioned at the edge of the circuit at the final corner, Turn 15, to mark the beginning of the pit entry.

Under the Race Director's Competition Notes, any driver who ran wide and passed to the right of the bollard was deemed to have entered the pit lane and was required to continue through it rather than return to the circuit.

The arrangement immediately created difficulties during the opening two practice sessions.

Liam Lawson and Valtteri Bottas were both shown black-and-white flags in FP1 for failing to follow the instruction and remaining on the circuit after passing the bollard.

Kimi Antonelli suffered the same fate in FP2, while his Mercedes team-mate George Russell complied with the instruction when he ran wide and entered the pits.

The incidents highlighted the potential consequences of the positioning should the same situation arise during the race, particularly given the possibility of a driver running wide at the final corner while battling another car.

The FIA has therefore amended the Race Director's notes overnight and moved the bollard further back.

The change means drivers who run wide at Turn 15 will now be able to remain on the circuit without having to negotiate the bollard and commit to the pit lane.

title: Mercedes facing complex challenge after F1 upgrade mysteriously underwhelms
excerpt:
As always, the results from the two free practice sessions on the first day of the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia should be treated with a degree of caution.

Nevertheless, what emerged, particularly from Mercedes in FP2, where the team was running a heavily revised car from an aerodynamic perspective, surprised many members of the paddock at the Sepang International Circuit.

George Russell and Kimi Antonelli finished seventh and eighth, respectively, around half a second behind Charles Leclerc, who topped the timing boards.

FP1 was essentially used to validate the new development package, represented primarily by new sidepods and a revised floor.

The team conducted constant-speed runs to gather useful data on track, which could then be compared with the predictive data from the simulations.

Therefore, it was no surprise that neither W17 had made a particular impression and, above all, that its actual race pace could not be properly assessed.

The mission for FP3

The situation was different, however, in the second free practice session. Both Russell and Antonelli tried various dynamic adjustments — namely suspension changes — as well as modifications to flap angles, without actually finding a satisfactory solution.

In practice, the dynamic response of the W17 to the new aerodynamic maps — namely the distribution of the downforce generated — was not consistent with what had been shown in the simulations.

Simply put, Mercedes could not strike a satisfactory balance, one that would allow either driver to extract the maximum performance from the car.

This may have been partly influenced by the fact — although this applies to everyone — that the track is subject to quite significant evolution due to the characteristics of the circuit and asphalt, compounded by the high ambient temperatures.

The fact remains that, ahead of FP3 and, above all, qualifying, the team's engineers have to start from scratch in determining the correct setup for the W17, having effectively failed to gather any clear reference points during the first day.

It is a complex challenge, but not an impossible one. In any case, it demonstrates how the introduction of large development packages is not always without its difficulties, particularly when the modifications alter the distribution of the downforce generated by the car, as is the case here.

This does not, however, mean that the evolution brought to Sepang does not work and should therefore be rejected.

Essentially, these are integration issues between the 'old and new', requiring an understanding of the W17's behaviour, which is different from before, in order to find new parameters that can be used for the setup.

title: Red Bull explain unusual Max Verstappen running in F1 rarity
excerpt:
Red Bull technical director Pierre Waché has identified promising signs for the team after a strong opening day at the Sepang International Circuit, despite brutal conditions during Friday practice for the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Max Verstappen topped FP1 with a 1:37.520s, before Isack Hadjar backed that up with second place in FP2, just 0.099s shy of Charles Leclerc's benchmark time. Verstappen rounded out the second session in fourth.

The four-time F1 champion's FP1 time, however, was the quickest of the day, and unusually he was one of only two drivers not to use a set of soft compound tyres in the second session.

The timesheets came against a backdrop of extreme heat, with ambient temperatures exceeding 33 degrees Celsius and track temperatures climbing to almost 62 degrees early in FP2.

The circuit, hosting Formula 1 for the first time since 2017, was also notably dusty and low on grip due to the lack of recent rubbering-in, with the abrasive original asphalt from nine years ago now sitting alongside a newer resurfaced section between Turns 6 and 12, creating inconsistent grip levels across a single lap.

Waché described the session as a steep challenge for both car and tyres, with the key opportunity for Red Bull lying in the learning process the team can extract from such a demanding and unfamiliar track.

"It was very warm, very difficult for the car and for the tyres," Waché said after FP2. "And also, there had not been much running on the track before our sessions.

"The track was quite dusty, and the grip evolved a lot, and the temperature was very high; track [temperature] reached 60 degrees, which we have never achieved with this type of [F1] car yet.

"It was difficult. The balance of the car is also tricky, but it's a learning process for the weekend."

Verstappen bucking the trend

Verstappen's FP2 programme notably omitted any running on the soft compound, a decision Waché put down to prioritising race preparation over outright pace.

"The main priority was to do a long run on medium that we didn't do this morning [in FP1]," he added to explain Verstappen's lack of soft tyre usage.

"Then, with the risk of rain in the middle of FP2, we didn't want to risk getting the long run in, and we switched to [it] very quickly. After that, we didn't have time to do the soft run."

Hadjar, meanwhile, was heard complaining over team radio about brake oscillations during his running.

Waché linked the issue to the unique demands the Sepang layout places on the braking system, with its two long straights feeding into heavy braking zones at Turn 1 and Turn 15 that place simultaneous strain on brake cooling and tyre thermal management.

"He had a difficult time with energy management and how you use the brakes on this track," Waché explained. "But hopefully we will sort out this problem."

title: Envision launches new Formula E livery against out-of-this-world backdrop
excerpt:
Envision took the unveiling of its Formula E Gen4 livery to a very special destination in the United States.

Envision has revealed its Season 13 livery under its new identity as Paysafe Envision Formula E Team, blending the squad's trademark green with the colours of new title partner Paysafe.

The launch took place in Jacksonville, Florida, the US base for the global payments firm, with fresh images of the car shot against the backdrop of the space launch complex at Cape Canaveral.

The team said the location was chosen to tie the new era to the same spirit of innovation and engineering ambition behind rocket launches.

The livery marks the team's new partnership with Paysafe, which serves millions of customers across gaming, entertainment and e-commerce.

Built around the sharper lines of Formula E's new Gen4 car, the design introduces a three-colour scheme of blue, white and green intended to sharpen the car's look on track, particularly when in motion.

The Gen4 car itself represents a major step up for the series, offering up to 450kW in race mode, 600kW in Attack Mode and 700kW of regenerative capability, translating to more than 612bhp, 815bhp and 951bhp respectively. Energy capacity has risen 43 percent compared to Gen3, to 55kWh, while the car now runs permanent all-wheel drive.

Franz Jung, VP of Envision Energy and CEO and chairman of the board of the Formula E outfit, said Season 13 marked a fresh start for the outfit.

"Season 13 marks the beginning of a really exciting new chapter for the team," said Jung. "We have a new name, new drivers, a new generation of Formula E car and a fantastic new partnership with Paysafe, so there is a real sense of momentum around the team.

title: Liam Lawson identifies crucial trick key to potential Bahrain GP success
excerpt:
Liam Lawson believes that successfully mastering tyre management at the Bahrain GP will be "key" to unlocking a strong result.

Lawson placed inside the top 10 in both Free Practice sessions in Sepang as the circuit plays host to the Bahrain GP in the first F1 race at the venue since the final Malaysian GP in 2017.

Throughout the two 60-minute sessions, drivers found track conditions tough, with the track temperature rising to around 62 degrees Celsius in FP2, with air temperature of around 34 degrees.

This, coupled with the rough and abrasive track surface, is causing major tyre wear, with stones picked up by the tyres, with a potential three-stop race expected in dry conditions.

Reflecting on his first experience at Sepang, Lawson identified tyre management as the foundation on which the rest of the weekend would be built upon.

"It was a fairly positive day here at the Bahrain GP," said Lawson.

"The track is fun to drive but very hard on tyres, particularly given the fact it hasn't been resurfaced in a few years.

"It's also extremely hot in Malaysia, which is physically tough. However, our training and preparation should put us in a strong position ahead of qualifying, where tyre management will be key."

Team boss revelation

title: Lewis Hamilton seeking Ferrari 'compromise' after tricky F1 discovery
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton is seeking the "right compromise" in his Ferrari after a tricky return to Sepang.

Hamilton placed only fifth in FP2 during Friday practice for the Bahrain GP in Malaysia, with team-mate Charles Leclerc topping the Briton by 0.305s, with both Red Bulls and Lando Norris sandwiched between the two Ferraris.

This followed FP1, where Hamilton placed sixth and was 0.223s down on Leclerc, who was fourth, as the 2014 Malaysian GP winner was left with work to do on grand prix racing's return to Sepang.

The track surface has been described as "sandpaper" and made conditions tricky for drivers as it overheats the tyres and makes controlling pace tricky, with Hamilton explaining that his target was to evaluate set-up choices and home in on the correct choice ahead of qualifying.

"It was a challenging day overall, with very little grip available on track," said Hamilton.

"Finding the right balance wasn’t easy, but that appeared to be a common theme across the field.

"Throughout the sessions we explored a couple of different set‑up directions, and now the focus is on understanding the data and identifying the right compromise.

"We don’t seem too far off the pace, but we know there’s still work to do to put the car in a better place for tomorrow."

title: Charles Leclerc highlights peril awaiting F1 drivers in Sepang
excerpt:
A number of F1 drivers complained about the tyre degradation that they faced during practice in Malaysia on Friday.

Charles Leclerc has stated he expects tyre degradation to remain a significant factor throughout the Bahrain Grand Prix at Sepang this weekend.

Drivers were subjected to significant tyre wear on Friday as they got up to speed at the Sepang International Circuit.

The track surface and high temperatures created a challenge for the competitors, which saw tyre performance quickly slip away during their stints.

But with similar conditions expected throughout the weekend, Leclerc is not expecting the situation to get any better.

"The high degradation is going to be a big thing for the race because tyres are not lasting for very long," Leclerc said.

"I don't expect this to get significantly better throughout the weekend.

"The grip in itself will most likely get better, but still, it's going to be a tricky weekend, particularly for the degradation.

"We normally have a good race car, so I hope that will be the case this weekend."

Charles Leclerc

Leclerc had to relearn Malaysia F1 track

Although Leclerc was not a full-time F1 driver when the sport last raced in Sepang in 2017, he took part in FP1 with Sauber that weekend, adding to his experience from a GP3 round the previous year.

But with some time passing between those outings, Leclerc admitted he had to relearn the circuit.

"I had to relearn the track all over again," he said. "I didn't remember it so well coming here.

"I had done one FP1, and then was all the way back to 2016 in GP3, where I had a race weekend.

"But it's a nice track, I enjoyed it. However, today the conditions were very, very, very poor, and so it was very slippery.

"For that we need to be good at anticipating what it will feel like tomorrow once the track is in a better condition."

Arvid Lindblad has confirmed that Racing Bulls held internal discussions after his collision with team-mate Liam Lawson at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, and says he knows what he needs to change in future.

I don't really know what gap he was looking for in the middle of both of us going into Turn 1; I just don't understand it," he said at the time. title: Fred Vasseur 'driver protection' crucial after 'taking a beating' at Ferrari
excerpt:
1997 F1 champion Jacques Villeneuve believes Fred Vasseur has an added layer of protection when it comes to his job scrutiny due to his support from the drivers.

Both Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc have asserted on multiple occasions that they believe Vasseur is the right figure to lead the team.

Ferrari has not been able to launch a serious title threat in many years, and Villeneuve insisted the team principal has to take responsibility for that.

"The team principal is never the scapegoat, he's the top of the organisation," Villeneuve told Sky F1.

"When things go well, he looks great. When things don't go well, he's the one who takes the beating."

Ferraru scrutiny 'the price you pay' for joining team

Ferrari is known to have increased pressure on its shoulders due to its status as the sport's most historic and successful team.

Villeneuve insisted that every individual who joins the organisation knows the weight that comes with it.

"Anyone who goes to Ferrari, not only a team principal, knows that's the price to pay," he said.

"It comes with a heavy baggage of you're fantastic when you perform, but two or three bad races, and the world is against you.

"It's been like that forever. It's been like that for other team principals, drivers, engineers, everyone.

"That's just the price to pay for being in the greatest team of all time."

"He's had more time than a lot of other ones already. The big difference now is he's protected by the drivers as well, which is a good thing."

title: George Russell voices weakened Mercedes upgrade fear after ominous signs
excerpt:
George Russell has warned that Mercedes' long-awaited aerodynamic upgrade is being 'neutralised' by extreme tyre overheating at the Sepang International Circuit, after the start to the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia fell short of lofty pre-event expectations.

Russell was second quickest in FP1, finishing almost four-tenths of a second shy of Max Verstappen's benchmark time, but the Briton slipped to seventh in FP2, just ahead of team-mate Kimi Antonelli, as the W17 struggled.

Speaking after Friday's running, Russell explained how the Sepang conditions were working against the new parts bolted onto the car.

"With these warm conditions, combined with the aggressive tarmac and the characteristics of the circuit, the tyre degradation throughout practice was high," Russell said after FP2.

"That was as we expected coming into the weekend, but with the amount of overheating on the tyres, it slightly neutralises the performance of any extra downforce we've added with our update.

"The cars are operating in quite a different window to what we usually do, and I don't think we quite got ours into the place that we needed today.

"We will look to get on top of that overnight, and hopefully, if we do so, we can be in the fight at the front for the rest of the weekend."

Shovlin flags long-run concern

Mercedes brought its most substantial upgrade since the Canadian Grand Prix in May to Sepang, with seven new components including a reworked floor, diffuser, sidepod profile, rear suspension fairings and brake duct winglets.

Some paddock estimates suggested the package would deliver a gain of around three-tenths of a second per lap, although any advantage has been offset by the W17's tyre wear difficulties thus far.

Indeed, those projections looked some way off after Friday's sessions, with trackside engineering director Andrew Shovlin confirming the team had struggled to extract the anticipated step.

"We were running the latest update package on both cars today, but rather than seeing the step in lap time that we had hoped for, we have been chasing a tricky balance and a fair amount of tyre overheating," Shovlin added.

"We had a few test items on the cars in FP1 that might have clouded the situation, but for FP2, we had both cars in a representative configuration, and it looked like we were still trailing, especially to the Red Bull.

"We've got some good ideas for setup changes to investigate during the overnight simulator work and will continue to analyse today's data to understand why we seem to lack a bit of pace.

"We're optimistic that with such a new package, these analyses will bear some fruit. The headline times are not especially representative, and we should be able to make some relatively easy progress on the single lap pace.

"Our concern is more the long run, where we seemed unusually offset on pace, and that is going to be the more challenging problem to solve."

title: Andretti announce shock Formula E team principal change in big announcement
excerpt:
Andretti has made a huge change to its Formula E leadership with one of the championship's most recognisable figures moving into a new role.

Andretti has named Campbell Hobson as its new team principal, succeeding Roger Griffiths ahead of the 2026/27 Formula E season.

Griffiths will not leave the organisation. Instead, he moves into a senior advisory role supporting both Andretti Formula E and the wider TWG Motorsports portfolio.

The Briton has led Andretti's Formula E operation since the championship's very first season back in 2014, meaning his spell in charge spanned 12 campaigns. U

nder his watch, the team picked up 13 race wins, 46 podiums and a drivers' title with Jake Dennis in 2023, while navigating multiple generations of car and several manufacturer partnerships along the way.

Hobson takes over having already played a central role in the team's day-to-day running. The Australian worked closely alongside Griffiths overseeing operations, personnel and on-track performance, meaning the promotion is being framed as a natural step rather than a shake-up.

Jill Gregory, President of Andretti Global and chief operating officer of TWG Motorsports, explained the thinking behind the appointment.

"Campbell has been instrumental in the operation, and we are very happy to see him take this opportunity to lead the team," said Gregory.

"He knows the program inside and out, has the respect of the team and brings the leadership and competitive drive we need as we look toward the future."

Roger Griffiths feels 'right time' for leadership change

It is a significant change for Andretti, with Griffiths being one of the most recognisable figures in the Formula E paddock.

Griffiths reflected on his 12 years building the programme from scratch, and why now felt like the moment to step back from the day-to-day.

"Leading this team from the beginning has been one of the great privileges of my career, and I'm incredibly proud of what we've built," said Griffiths.

"After 12 seasons, this feels like the right time to pass the torch. Campbell has been a trusted part of our leadership for years and understands this organization at every level; he has earned this opportunity. I'm excited to support him while also contributing more broadly across Andretti and TWG Motorsports."

Gregory added that Griffiths' impact went well beyond the results sheet.

"Roger has been foundational to this program," said Gregory. "What he has built over 12 seasons extends well beyond results on track into an exceptional team and culture. This transition allows us to build on that foundation while continuing to benefit from Roger's experience and perspective in a broader capacity."

Hobson's first season in charge arrives at a pivotal moment for the team, with Formula E entering its Gen4 era. Andretti will field Jake Dennis and Felipe Drugovich again, now running as a customer outfit partnered with Nissan.

Hobson, for his part, said he was grateful for the opportunity and had big shoes to fill.

"It's an incredible privilege to take on the role of Team Principal," said Hobson. "I have tremendous respect for Roger and what he has built, and I'm grateful for the team's trust and this opportunity. We have a great group of people, a strong foundation and a lot of ambition for what comes next."
